title: Data Types & EDA
html:
Exploratory data analysis (EDA) is how you learn what's in the data before modelling: types, missing values, distributions, outliers, the target's balance and suspicious features.

Kinds of data

Structured (tabular) data has rows and named columns — database tables, CSVs. Unstructured data — text, images, audio, video — has no predefined columns; classic ML needs features extracted from it, while deep learning learns them. Within a table, each column has a statistical type that decides how it is prepared:

TypeExamplesTypical preparation
Numerical — continuousPrice, temperature, durationScaling; log-transform if skewed
Numerical — discrete (counts)Number of purchases, childrenAs numbers; sometimes capped or log-transformed
Categorical — nominal (no order)City, product id, colourOne-hot, target or hash encoding
Categorical — ordinal (ordered)Size S < M < L, education level, star ratingOrdered integer codes
BinaryIs_premium, has_children0 / 1
Date / timeSignup timestampExtract parts (hour, weekday), elapsed time, cyclical encoding
Free textReviews, titlesBag-of-words / TF-IDF, embeddings
IdentifiersUser id, row numberUsually not features — they let a model memorise rows

A first look with pandas

EDA checklist

CheckHowWhy
Shape, types, idsdf.info(), df.dtypesNumbers stored as strings, ids that must not be features
Missing valuesdf.isna().mean()Choose imputation; missingness can be informative
Duplicatesdf.duplicated().sum()Duplicates across train/test inflate scores
Target distributionvalue_counts(normalize=True) / histogramClass imbalance, skewed regression targets
Univariate distributionsdescribe(), histograms, box plotsSkew, impossible values (age = −1), outliers
RelationshipsScatter plots, corr(), grouped means by categoryUseful features, collinearity
Too-good featuresA single feature almost perfectly predicting the targetUsually target leakage
TimePlot counts and target rate over timeDrift, seasonality, logging changes
Watch out

Do the detailed EDA on the training split. Looking closely at the test set and designing features around it leaks information about it into your choices.

Correlation, carefully

  • Pearson measures linear association only; zero correlation does not mean independence.
  • Spearman uses ranks — robust to outliers and captures any monotonic trend.
  • Correlation is not causation: ice-cream sales and drownings both rise in summer.
  • For categorical–target relationships, compare target rates per category or use mutual information.
What do you look at first in a new dataset?

Size and column types, the target's distribution, missing values and duplicates, obviously wrong values, then each feature's distribution and its relationship with the target. I also check how the data was collected and over what time span, and flag any feature that predicts the target suspiciously well.

Why shouldn't an ID column be used as a feature?

It carries no generalisable information but is unique per row, so flexible models memorise it and look great on training data. Worse, if ids were assigned in time order, it can leak time or target information.
